candidateRows: Six philosophical and scientific explanations together constitute a cumulative case for the existence of God.
This states Craig's overarching exterior case and identifies the principal explanatory arguments offered in support of the debate's theistic position.
After distinguishing trusting God from believing that God exists, Craig introduces exterior arguments and summarizes six lines of theistic explanation.
The resurrection hypothesis best explains four widely accepted historical facts and thereby supports Christian theism.
The move supplies the principal bridge from generic arguments for God to the specifically Christian conclusion included in the debate motion.
Craig attributes divine claims to Jesus, enumerates four historical facts concerning Jesus's fate, and argues that resurrection best explains them.
Personal experience of God can rationally ground Christian belief as properly basic without dependence on exterior arguments.
This establishes an independent epistemic route to Christian belief, making the theistic position less dependent on success in the public evidential arguments.
Craig observes that many believers lack resources to investigate formal arguments and instead ground faith in an experienced relationship with God.
Big Bang evidence does not establish a first moment, leaving the universe's alleged beginning scientifically uncertain.
The move directly challenges the crucial beginning-of-the-universe premise underlying the cosmological argument by separating observed expansion from an absolute origin.
Craig's claim that God best explains the universe's absolute beginning in the finite past.
O'Connor reconstructs the cosmological argument, distinguishes the observed hot dense state from a first moment, and notes disputed singularity assumptions.
Actual infinities and Hilbert's Hotel are counterintuitive rather than contradictory, so intuition does not establish their impossibility.
This attacks the philosophical basis for the universe-began-to-exist premise by denying that the characteristic consequences of actual infinity amount to contradictions.
Craig's contention that an infinite past is impossible because completing an infinite series cannot yield the present.
After rehearsing the traversal argument and Hilbert's Hotel, O'Connor distinguishes alternative meanings of fullness and argues that extreme cases unsettle intuition.
The traversal objection lacks a well-defined infinite unit, and presentism makes classifying the nonexistent past as an actual infinity unclear.
The move challenges both key assumptions of the philosophical beginning argument: what forms the infinite collection and whether a past sequence is actually infinite.
Craig's argument that reaching the present would require traversing an actually infinite collection of past events.
O'Connor questions whether events, moments, or conventional time units supply the relevant collection, then contrasts presentist and tenseless theories of time.
A beginningless past would require an actual infinity formed by successive addition, rendering temporal traversal impossible.
This defends the principal philosophical support for a finite past by separating two infinity arguments and specifying equal standard events as the traversed units.
O'Connor's objections that actual infinity is merely unintuitive and that the traversed temporal units are undefined.
Craig distinguishes the impossibility of instantiated actual infinities from formation by successive addition, uses a modified Zeno analogy, and defines standard events conventionally.
Aristotle's potentially infinite past is conceptually mistaken because a completed earlier sequence differs from an indefinitely growing future.
The move answers a historically important counterexample invoked against the infinity argument and clarifies why future endlessness does not imply a beginningless past.
O'Connor's appeal to Aristotle as accepting an eternal past while rejecting actual infinities in reality.
Craig defines actual infinity as complete and potential infinity as indefinitely increasing, then argues that only a future sequence can fit the latter description.
Contemporary astrophysical evidence makes a finite cosmic past more probable, and limiting the Big Bang label to the early hot dense state does not eliminate an initial boundary.
This supplies the principal scientific confirmation for the Kalam premise that the universe began to exist and answers a cited cosmological objection.
O'Connor's appeal to scientific usage that treats the Big Bang as an early hot dense state rather than an initial singularity.
After distinguishing actual from potential infinity, Craig turns to scientific support for cosmic finitude and answers the earlier characterization of Big Bang cosmology.
A finite cosmic past does not require an initial singularity because singularity-free models such as the Hartle-Hawking proposal can still have a beginning.
The distinction protects the beginning premise from objections that singularity resolution by quantum cosmology removes every relevant cosmic beginning.
The objection that rejecting or resolving an initial cosmological singularity defeats the claim that the universe had a finite past.
Craig supplements his astrophysical case by separating a beginning from a singular point and uses a specific quantum model to illustrate the distinction.
The universe's low-entropy condition supports a beginning because a closed universe with an infinite past should already have reached thermodynamic equilibrium or heat death.
This is an independent scientific line supporting the finite-past premise and therefore materially strengthens the cumulative Kalam cosmological case.
Following the astrophysical expansion argument, Craig adds thermodynamics and the low-entropy past hypothesis as a separate confirmation of cosmic beginning.
Craig's event-counting argument is undermined by arbitrary temporal units, relativistic time, and the apparent symmetry between nonexistent past and future under presentism.
The move challenges the conceptual foundation of Craig's argument against an infinite past and identifies the theory-of-time assumption on which it depends.
Craig's claim that choosing any conventional interval allows a beginningless past to be counted as an actually infinite collection of elapsed events.
O'Connor begins with examples of division and relativity, disputes objective temporal units, and then raises the A-theory versus B-theory dependence of the Kalam.
The tensed A-theory treats temporal becoming as objective, whereas the B-theory denies it; Craig defends the former while noting that some proponents formulate the Kalam even on the latter.
This identifies and defends the metaphysical framework behind Craig's treatment of elapsed events while limiting the claim that the Kalam wholly depends on it.
O'Connor's contention that the Kalam relies on a disputed A-theory of time and does not work if the tenseless B-theory is true.
In response to the theory-of-time challenge, Craig defines tensed and tenseless views, states his commitment to temporal becoming, and mentions B-theoretic Kalam defenses.
If neither past nor future exists under presentism, God's complete present knowledge of an endless future makes denying that future the actuality granted to the completed past appear unjustified.
The objection targets Craig's proposed past-future asymmetry by using theistic foreknowledge to make both temporal directions equally conceptually determinate.
Craig's distinction between the completed and actualized past and the merely potential future under a tensed theory of temporal becoming.
O'Connor presses why a nonexistent past counts as actual while a nonexistent but fully foreknown future does not, framing each as conceptually available to God.
Even if the set of all future events is actually infinite conceptually, its concrete temporal instantiation remains finite at every stage and only potentially infinite.
This directly answers the divine-foreknowledge objection by separating an abstractly specified infinite set from a concretely realized temporal sequence.
O'Connor's argument that God's complete knowledge makes the endless future conceptually actual in the same relevant sense as the elapsed past.
Craig concedes for argument that the future-event set may be infinite, but argues that successive realization always yields only finite stages tending toward infinity.
The same successive-instantiation reasoning applies when counting past days, so presentism alone does not explain why an infinite sequence may extend forward but not backward.
This concise reversal attacks the alleged asymmetry on which Craig's response depends and returns the burden to the metaphysics of temporal direction.
Craig's claim that instantiating future events one at a time can produce only a potentially infinite sequence and never an actually infinite concrete totality.
O'Connor argues that one-by-one counting is potential in either direction and asks why a present-only ontology permits endless forward extension but forbids the past analogue.
Time is asymmetric because temporal becoming has one unique later-than direction, providing a relevant difference between an endless future and a beginningless past.
The proposed direction of temporal becoming is Craig's explicit answer to the central symmetry objection against allowing an endless future while rejecting an infinite past.
O'Connor's challenge that if only the present exists, the same potential-infinity reasoning should permit extension both forward and backward in time.
Craig replies that temporal directions differ and that becoming proceeds uniquely toward later events, which he presents as the missing past-future symmetry breaker.
An omniscient God presently knows the contents of infinitely many future temporal intervals, apparently placing an actually infinite range of physical referents within divine cognition.
The objection seeks an internal tension between Craig's rejection of concretely instantiated actual infinities and his commitments about omniscience and an endless future.
Craig's distinction between an actually infinite conceptual set of future events and the merely potentially infinite concrete sequence realized over time.
After Craig invokes temporal asymmetry, O'Connor focuses on omniscience and argues that God's present apprehension already ranges over infinitely many future physical events.
Standard human-centered theodicies do not explain the immense suffering imposed on non-human animals throughout evolutionary history.
This introduces animal suffering as the principal evidential challenge to theism and establishes the subject governing most of the remaining exchange.
Craig's opening arguments that cosmology, morality, and other evidence make Christian theism more probable.
After choosing suffering over another Kalam exchange, O'Connor argues that free will, soul-making, the fall, and higher-order goods do not account for evolutionary animal suffering.
Animal suffering is more probable on theism than naturalism because fine-tuning makes sentient life itself vastly more probable on theism.
The move attempts to reverse the evidential force of the central objection by embedding suffering within the comparative probability of sentient life.
O'Connor's contention that evolutionary animal suffering is powerful evidence against a good and powerful God.
Craig reframes the issue comparatively: naturalism allegedly makes any life, especially sentient life capable of suffering, far less likely than theism does.
Appealing to fine-tuning sidesteps whether animal suffering itself decreases the probability of God when that datum is considered in isolation.
This challenges Craig's comparative reframing and restores the disputed datum's independent evidential relevance to the existence and character of God.
Craig's claim that suffering favors theism because naturalism makes sentient life antecedently much less probable.
O'Connor grants a law-governed universe for purposes of analysis and argues that disagreement over fine-tuning should not prevent asking why God permits animal suffering.
An evolutionary world containing extensive suffering may be necessary for the optimal number of people freely to attain eternal salvation.
This supplies Craig's substantive theodicy for evolutionary suffering rather than relying solely on the fine-tuning comparison or burden of proof.
O'Connor's demand for a reason why God would permit animal suffering apart from the fine-tuning argument.
Craig proposes that God's overriding purpose is human salvation and invokes butterfly effects to argue that observers cannot judge particular suffering gratuitous.
An omnipotent God should not be constrained by evolutionary history or fossil fuels when creating free humans capable of salvation.
The objection attacks the proposed theodicy at its foundation by arguing that divine omnipotence defeats the alleged necessity of suffering-producing conditions.
Craig's proposal that evolutionary suffering and its causal consequences may be required for optimal human salvation.
O'Connor questions why God would be bound by a precarious causal chain in which an unseen animal's suffering contributes indispensably to salvation.
The atheist cannot show that a morally perfect God lacks sufficient reasons for choosing an evolutionary world containing natural and moral evil.
This combines skeptical theism with a burden-of-proof defense, insulating the proposed theodicy from claims that alternative possible worlds seem preferable.
O'Connor's objection that divine omnipotence should permit salvation without the particular suffering-producing evolutionary history.
Craig stresses uncertainty about alternative worlds, cites the role of evolutionary history in civilization, rejects deceptive apparent-age creation, and assigns atheism the burden.
God could preserve animals' ecological functions while withholding sentience, thereby avoiding their pain without disrupting evolutionary outcomes.
The proposal offers a concrete alternative world intended to defeat the claim that animal consciousness and pain are necessary for ecological functionality.
Craig's contention that proposed alternative worlds are speculative and may not realize God's salvific purposes.
O'Connor argues that behaviorally complex animals could react mechanically without consciousness, making their suffering avoidable even if their ecological roles remained unchanged.
Animal pleasure does not cancel the evidential problem because apparently unnecessary suffering remains unexpected even when a life is pleasant overall.
This rebuts a significant audience-supported defense that animal lives are sufficiently happy and clarifies that compensation does not explain gratuitous suffering.
The audience questioner's suggestion that animals delight in life and that O'Connor overemphasizes their suffering.
O'Connor argues that wild suffering probably outweighs pleasure, but adds that even abundant pleasure would not explain why severe avoidable suffering exists.
Animal suffering is less severe than critics assume because animals generally live contented lives and lack human-like second-order awareness of pain.
The move directly reduces the alleged scale and qualitative severity of the debate's central animal-suffering evidence against Christian theism.
O'Connor's claim that animal pleasure neither outweighs nor explains the extensive suffering found in nature.
Craig says animals are typically content until sudden predation and argues that projecting human feelings onto them ignores their lack of reflexive awareness.
Distrusting human moral intuitions about divine cruelty undermines the moral argument, which itself relies on those intuitions to establish objective morality.
This presents an internal consistency objection connecting the suffering defense to a separate major argument for God, making the reply motion-level in consequence.
The audience challenge that humans should not project their limited moral knowledge and standards onto a non-human divine being.
O'Connor argues that theism credits God with supplying reliable moral intuitions, then selectively asks people to abandon those intuitions concerning suffering and scripture.
A world containing extensive natural and moral evil may be necessary to maximize the number of people who freely embrace God and salvation.
The move supplies Craig's principal justification for divine permission of suffering and assigns the atheist a demanding feasible-world comparison.
The audience challenge that an omnipotent God could have created animals without pervasive pain and suffering.
After an audience member asks why God created a world containing animal suffering, Craig argues that evil may be tied to optimal free acceptance of salvation.
Biblical cases in which God commands or causes animal harm intensify the problem beyond suffering that God merely permits.
The distinction between permitted suffering and divinely commanded harm directly challenges the moral character of the Christian God under debate.
Craig's answer treating the audience question as the familiar problem of why God permits pain and suffering.
O'Connor redirects the exchange from general permission of evil to scriptural depictions of commanded animal harm and alleged failures of divine stewardship.
The extreme improbability of life-permitting constants under accident makes intelligent selection a more plausible explanation of cosmic fine-tuning.
This is a direct restatement of the explanatory inference at the heart of the debate's fine-tuning argument for an intelligent creator.
The audience objection that necessary constants grounded in God may be no more explanatory than necessary brute facts.
Craig answers by emphasizing the narrow life-permitting range of physical constants and contrasting accidental placement with intentional determination by a creator.
Appealing to divine will distinguishes God from a brute fact, but hostile meta-conditions for matter create tension with a creator intending a material world.
The move concedes a relevant explanatory difference while arguing that fine-tuning's background improbability undermines the proposed creator's material intention.
Craig's claim that intelligent determination better explains why the physical constants fall within a life-permitting range.
O'Connor says divine will can explain selected constants, then argues that conditions making matter exceptionally difficult appear contrary to a creator's intention.
Strong independent grounds for God's existence support the conclusion that apparently gratuitous suffering actually serves an unknown greater good.
This reverses the evidential problem of evil by making established theism a reason to deny that apparently purposeless suffering is genuinely gratuitous.
The questioner's claim that suffering is irrelevant once other arguments make a creator God's existence more probable.
Craig formalizes the exchange as competing logical directions: independent evidence for God can entail that suffering has a purpose despite human ignorance of it.
The problem of evil remains evidence against an all-loving God even if it does not refute every possible creator or erase all reasons for theism.
The move states O'Connor's overall agnostic position and clarifies the limited but direct evidential force of suffering against specifically loving theism.
Craig's argument that good independent grounds for God imply that apparently gratuitous suffering must serve a greater good.
O'Connor distinguishes reasons for generic theism from reasons to doubt an all-loving God, while stressing the limited debate time devoted to suffering and Kalam.
Suffering is evidentially relevant to Christian theism because Christianity describes a personally concerned, saving God rather than an indifferent first cause.
The move identifies the divine attributes that make suffering probabilistically relevant and connects them directly to resurrection, salvation, and mental welfare.
The audience participant's insistence that suffering is irrelevant and that belief in a creator must be decided by wholly separate arguments.
O'Connor argues that indifference to suffering might fit an impersonal creator but conflicts with the worshipped Christian God who acts for human salvation.
People can know God independently of philosophical and historical evidence through the inward witness and universal drawing of the Holy Spirit.
The claim supplies Craig's central answer to unequal historical access to arguments and grounds belief in God apart from intellectual opportunity.
The audience objection that a fair and loving God gives people radically unequal historical access to arguments and evidence.
Craig accepts that most Christians lacked philosophical or historical arguments but says divine self-disclosure gives every person an inward route to knowledge of God.
The evidential problem concerns suffering's apparently arbitrary distribution across birthplace and species, not merely the universal existence of some suffering.
The move sharpens the suffering objection by locating its force in unequal distribution, thereby resisting explanations aimed only at suffering in general.
Craig's appeal to universal divine drawing as an answer to concerns about unequal access, fairness, and salvation.
O'Connor distinguishes a universal rationale for suffering from the observed disparities produced by birthplace and species, which he treats as the deeper concern.
A God's-eye perspective makes past and future sufficiently comparable for the actual-infinite objection, whereas an exclusively human perspective would change the metaphysics.
The move revisits the temporal metaphysics underlying O'Connor's principal challenge to the Kalam argument and explains why theism affects that comparison.
The final question about whether God's-eye and human perspectives on time yield different metaphysical implications for the earlier dispute.
O'Connor says an existing divine perspective changes the comparison of past and future infinities, while a world containing only present-bound human perspectives would differ.
